byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: 203 million people, 108 million motor vehicles, and a fertility rate that had fallen from 3.7 births per woman to 2.5 in a decade.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 1970 census counted 203.3 million people, 57.5 to the square mile.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: Decennial census historical facts, 1970
World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A baby born in 1970 could expect to live nearly 71 years.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)
Our World in Data: Life expectancy (UN World Population Prospects and other series)

items.title: Town and city
items.summary: About 73.5 percent of Americans lived in urban areas.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Urban population (% of total)

items.title: Infant deaths
items.summary: About 20 of every 1,000 babies died before their first birthday.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)

items.title: Births per woman
items.summary: The fertility rate was 2.48 births per woman, down from 3.65 in 1960.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Fertility rate, total (births per woman)

items.title: Motor vehicles
items.summary: Registrations reached 108.4 million: 89.2 million cars, 18.8 million trucks and 378,000 buses.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations
FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: Motor vehicle registrations

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1970 prices, appliance counts or meals: the pages we opened on fast food and groceries had no figures for 1970.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: The long midi skirt that stores stocked in 1970 mostly stayed on the racks, while women moved to trousers and jeans.

items.title: The midi that did not sell
items.summary: In 1970 the industry tried to move women from miniskirts to calf-length midi skirts; women, especially in the United States, refused to buy them, which the article says almost ruined the American fashion industry.

items.title: Minis through 1972
items.summary: Many women kept wearing miniskirts through 1972; more switched to trousers and jeans than to the longer skirts.

items.title: Trousers everywhere
items.summary: By the early 1970s women wore pants in every setting, jeans included, making it the first decade in Western fashion when they wore more trousers than skirts.

items.title: Bell-bottoms, hot pants and sideburns
items.summary: Bell-bottoms were popular for women and men, hot pants and long sideburns were popular in 1971, and platform shoes were widespread among women and young people.

items.title: A flood of synthetics
items.summary: Overproduction flooded the market with affordable synthetic clothing; Vogue noted in the early 1970s that 'there are no rules in the fashion game now'.

sensitivity.note: This item touches on war, famine, epidemic disease or disaster.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: A production worker in manufacturing earned about $133 a week, and a new law set federal workplace safety rules.

items.title: A manufacturing paycheque
items.summary: A production worker in manufacturing earned $3.35 an hour, or $133.33 a week, on average; in durable goods $143.07 and in non-durable goods $120.43.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4361-4366: Hourly and weekly earnings of production workers in manufacturing, 1909-1995

items.title: A law for safety at work
items.summary: President Nixon signed the Occupational Safety and Health Act on 29 December 1970.

workAndWages.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures for 1970 hours, women's work or the minimum wage.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: The school year was 179 days, and children took part in the first Earth Day.

items.title: The school year
items.summary: The average school term was 178.9 days, a pupil attended 161.7 of them, and 90.4 percent of enrolled pupils were present on a given day.

sources.label: NCES Digest of Education Statistics 2003, Table 36: school term and attendance, 1869-70 to 1999-2000

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced enrolment figures, costs or toy sales for 1970.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: The jumbo jet entered service in January, and three new small American cars went on sale.

items.title: The jumbo jet
items.summary: Pan Am began the first Boeing 747 service, New York to London, on 22 January 1970; the aircraft typically seats 366 passengers in three classes and 92 were delivered during 1970.

items.title: Three small cars
items.summary: AMC introduced the Gremlin on 1 April, Chevrolet the Vega on 10 September and Ford the Pinto on 11 September 1970.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: A postal strike stopped the mail in New York in March.

items.title: The postal strike
items.summary: A U.S. Postal Service strike began in New York City on 18 March 1970, spread to other cities and lasted about two weeks.

keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1970 postage rates, telephone counts or television households.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: Cigarette advertisements were ordered off television.

items.title: Cigarettes off the screen
items.summary: The Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act, signed on 1 April 1970, banned cigarette advertising on television from 1 January 1971.

healthAndMedicine.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1970 doctor fees, hospital costs or disease figures.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: New on the television that year: soap operas, football on Monday nights, a public network and a comedy about two roommates.

items.title: All My Children
items.summary: The soap opera All My Children premiered on ABC on 5 January 1970.

items.title: Monday Night Football
items.summary: Monday Night Football debuted on ABC on 21 September 1970.

items.title: The Odd Couple
items.summary: The Odd Couple premiered on ABC on 24 September 1970.

items.title: PBS
items.summary: National Educational Television closed and was succeeded by PBS, which began broadcasting on 5 October 1970.

items.title: The first New York City Marathon
items.summary: The first New York City Marathon was run on 13 September 1970.

spotlight.title: The first Earth Day and everyday environment
spotlight.standfirst: On 22 April 1970 an estimated 20 million Americans took part in rallies and teach-ins, and by December there was an Environmental Protection Agency.

items.title: Twenty million on 22 April
items.summary: An estimated 20 million Americans took part in rallies, marches and teach-ins on the first Earth Day, 22 April 1970.

items.title: A teach-in for campuses
items.summary: Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed the nationwide teach-in and hired Harvard graduate student Denis Hayes as national coordinator, choosing the date to draw college students.

items.title: Schools join in
items.summary: More than 10,000 primary and secondary schools took part, mostly in beach clean-ups, tree planting and recycling.

items.title: The EPA begins
items.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency began operating on 2 December 1970, after Nixon proposed it on 9 July; in its first year it had a budget of $1.4 billion and 5,800 employees.

items.title: A wave of laws
items.summary: After a campaign against a 'Dirty Dozen' of legislators, seven of whom lost, a wave of laws followed, including the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act; a major expansion of the Clean Air Act was approved in December 1970.
